stories.title: Libya: Landmark ICC Trial On Libya Migrant Abuses Must Lead to More Scrutiny of EU Complicity
stories.summary: Libya: Landmark ICC Trial On Libya Migrant Abuses Must Lead to More Scrutiny of EU Complicity Supplied From its early years, the International Criminal Court (ICC) was intended to serve as a court of last resort. It was meant to fill gaps where national systems fail. The limited success, alongside the clear focus of investigations and prosecutions on African countries while major powers remain outside its legal reach, has fueled persistent criticism. 25 August 2026 The New Humanitarian (Geneva) By Allison West and Viola Castellano Berlin — "Anyone who violates people's rights should face the consequences." In late July, judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unanimously voted to confirm charges against former Libyan security official Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri, paving the way for his case to move to trial. El Hishri stands accused of crimes against humanity and war crimes including imprisonment, torture, rape, murder, enslavement, and persecution against Libyan and non-Libyan detainees - among them migrants and refugees - at the notorious Mitiga prison in Libya's capital, Tripoli. The case - the first to reach trial since the ICC opened an investigation into international crimes committed in Libya 15 years ago - marks a major legal breakthrough, offering a long-awaited, if still partial, reckoning for survivors and Libyans more broadly with the system that enabled the abuses.

La Maison centrale de Conakry, dans la commune de Kaloum, est progressivement démolie depuis le samedi 22 août. D'abord inaugurée en 1903 - tandis que le bâtiment en cours de destruction date, lui, de 1933 - cette prison était devenue au fil des décennies l’un des lieux les plus emblématiques du système pénitentiaire guinéen. Après l'indépendance, elle a vu passer nombre d'acteurs politiques de premier plan, comme les ex-présidents Alpha Condé, Moussa Dadis Camara, ou encore le journaliste Souleymane Diallo. Frédéric Le Marcis, anthropologue à l'École normale supérieure de Lyon, revient sur l'histoire de cette prison et son usage politique pendant la période coloniale et après l'indépendance de 1958.

stories.title: Ghana: Erosion of Values Fuelling Galamsey, Sanitation Crisis - Chief of Staff

He said Ghana's current struggles with sanitation and environmental degradation were partly the result of Ghanaians abandoning traditional practices that promoted communal responsibility and respect for the environment. "We are now having issues with sanitation and struggling with galamsey because we have dropped our heritage," Mr Debrah said. He made the statement in Accra on Friday at the Clean Conference, held on the theme: 'Assessing Ghana's Progress Towards the UN SDGs.' stories.title: Uganda: Hundreds of Passengers Stranded As Taxi Crackdown Bites
stories.summary: Uganda: Hundreds of Passengers Stranded As Taxi Crackdown Bites Alex Esagala/Daily Monitor Traffic in Kampala (file photo). 25 August 2026 The Independent (Kampala) Kampala — Hundreds of passengers were left stranded across the Kampala metropolitan area on Monday as traffic police launched a crackdown on commuter taxis in dangerous mechanical condition. The operation, which began as early as 6:00 a.m., targeted dilapidated 14-seater taxis commonly known as "gganyegenya" operating in Kampala, Wakiso and Mukono districts. Police deployed heavily along major routes, including Gayaza Road, Jinja Road, the Northern Bypass at Busega, Namugongo, Kawempe and Hoima Road, stopping and impounding taxis found to be in dangerous mechanical condition. At Rubigi Police Station along Hoima Road, one of the busiest checkpoints, police impounded at least 40 taxis serving routes to Kakiri, Nansana-Gganda and Nansana-Nabweru, areas known for having large numbers of older taxis. Passengers were ordered to disembark and find alternative transport, while the impounded vehicles were towed by police recovery trucks to the Nakawa parking yard, which has been gazetted by Kampala Capital City Authority for impounded vehicles.

"The brutality of the war waged by the Rapid Support Forces [RSF] and the Sudanese Armed Forces has discredited their claims to be legitimate governors of the Sudanese people," said Boulos, who warned that "external financial and military support is fueling the conflict and risks drawing neighboring states deeper into war." Boulos said the US wants to expand the embargo geographically as well as materially in order to cover unmanned aerial vehicles and related technologies . The Darfur embargo has been in place for two decades and will expire on September 12, 2026, if not amended or renewed. An expansion would require a Security Council vote.

stories.title: Gabon : Albert Ondo Ossa, un « président élu » qui n’en démord pas
stories.summary: Gabon : Albert Ondo Ossa, un « président élu » qui n’en démord pas Depuis son exil parisien, Albert Ondo Ossa continue envers et contre tous de s’autoproclamer « président élu » de la présidentielle d’août 2023. Portrait d’un homme désormais bien seul, mais convaincu que l’histoire lui donnera raison. L’opposant gabonais Albert Onda Ossa, à Paris, en août 2026. Par Jeanne Le Bihan Publié le 24 août à 18h51, modifié hier à 09h45 Lecture : 5 minutes. Fichier généré le Lire dans l’app Il est loin d’être le premier, certes.

stories.title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses
stories.summary: A spokesperson for the Duke of Sussex, pictured at a national park in Malawi in 2019, said his commitment to conservation in Africa continued. Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PA View image in fullscreen A spokesperson for the Duke of Sussex, pictured at a national park in Malawi in 2019, said his commitment to conservation in Africa continued. Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PA Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy. Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee of African Parks , which admitted last year that human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo. The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.

stories.title: Mission to verify DRC-M23 ceasefire gets underway in South Kivu
stories.summary: A mission to verify a fragile ceasefire between the Congolese army and Rwanda-backed M23 armed group was deployed Monday to the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo as the two sides traded accusations of abuses.

stories.title: Protests erupt in Tunisia after migrant boat sinks
stories.summary: The Tunisian city of Ben Guerdane erupted in protest on Saturday night one day after a boat carrying 15 migrants sank off the country's southeastern coast. Protesters blocked roads and set fire to tyres after the news of the shipwreck was announced.

stories.title: Centrafrique-Tchad : Abdoulaye Miskine, un ancien chef de guerre bien encombrant
stories.summary: Affaibli après près de sept ans de détention, le chef rebelle centrafricain comparaît de nouveau, ce 24 août, devant la justice tchadienne. Au-delà de son sort judiciaire, c’est la question des fragiles relations entre Faustin-Archange Touadéra et Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno qui se joue.

stories.title: Video shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnapping
stories.summary: Nigerian millitary take part in a security drill in Nigeria as mass kidnappings become more common in some parts. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Nigerian millitary take part in a security drill in Nigeria as mass kidnappings become more common in some parts. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Video shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnapping Gunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older people An armed group has posted a video showing what ⁠residents said were about ⁠600 women, children and ​older people abducted in an attack on a mosque in Nigeria’s north-central Niger State last week. The video, posted on Facebook and WhatsApp, ⁠showed large groups of people seated in a forested area surrounded by armed men. Several children could be heard crying in the background.

stories.title: Deux casques bleus éthiopiens tués dans une embuscade au Soudan du Sud, selon l’ONU
stories.summary: Les deux soldats de la Minuss ont été tués dans une « embuscade tendue par des individus armés non identifiés » dans l’Etat de Jonglei, où les combats entre forces gouvernementales et milices d’opposition se sont intensifiés ces derniers mois.

stories.title: Zambia courts sealed off as election petition deadline looms
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the presidential election result in court By Dingindaba Buyoya Published 24 August 2026 Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches. An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access. Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%. Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others.

stories.title: '101-year-old great-grandmother' arrested for selling cannabis in Nigeria
stories.summary: Image source, NDLEA Image caption, Esther Ogunmabo said she started selling illicit drugs after her shop was destroyed in a fire By Mansur Abubakar Reporting from Abuja Published 24 August 2026 An elderly woman, who the authorities say is 101, has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly selling cannabis, in a case that has drawn widespread attention. Esther Ogunmabo, described as a great-grandmother, was apprehended on Saturday in Ogun state, in the south-west of the country, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced. Femi Babafemi, the agency's media director, said the centenarian was found with "retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals". The NDLEA said the suspect told investigators that she turned to the illicit drug trade after her provisions shop was destroyed by fire. According to the Ndlea, one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, allegedly arranged for the supply of the substance to her every four days.

stories.title: Transferts d’argent : Sendwave et TapTapSend, le duel africain des « digital natives »
stories.summary: Surfant sur l’essor du mobile money, les fintechs Sendwave et TapTapSend ont bousculé les transferts d’argent des diasporas vers l’Afrique. Elles s’affrontent sur le continent, mettant en avant rapidité des transactions et frais réduits.

stories.title: After 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s how | Jean Kaseya and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
stories.summary: Vanny Birungi, a Red Cross volunteer, speaks to people in Bunia, DRC, during a public awareness campaign 10 days after the Ebola outbreak was officially declared. Photograph: M Sawasawa/AP View image in fullscreen Vanny Birungi, a Red Cross volunteer, speaks to people in Bunia, DRC, during a public awareness campaign 10 days after the Ebola outbreak was officially declared. Photograph: M Sawasawa/AP After 100 days of the deadliest Ebola outbreak, it can be stopped. Here’s how Jean Kaseya and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus Ebola is a disease that spreads through communities, so we need to listen to communities if we want to halt its spread E ach time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we go first to listen. In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas.

stories.title: Bradley Mortin, politiste : « Au Sahel, les groupes djihadistes et criminels financent en partie leurs activités grâce à l’extraction de lithium »
stories.summary: Si l’Afrique ne produit qu’environ 15 % du lithium mondial, c’est sur le continent que le minerai a connu la plus forte hausse de production en 2025. Le chercheur estime, dans un entretien au « Monde », que cette ressource se transforme en un nouveau canal de financement du terrorisme.

stories.title: Children make up half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads
stories.summary: A child is vaccinated at a health centre in Quebo, Guinea-Bissau. There is a sense of urgency in the heath sector, with schools due to reopen in September. Photograph: Vincent Tremeau/Unicef View image in fullscreen A child is vaccinated at a health centre in Quebo, Guinea-Bissau. There is a sense of urgency in the heath sector, with schools due to reopen in September. Photograph: Vincent Tremeau/Unicef Children make up half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected More than half of the mpox cases reported in Guinea-Bissau have been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic.

stories.title: Football : l’Afrique pas si unie que cela derrière Gianni Infantino
stories.summary: Officiellement, la Confédération africaine de football (CAF) a apporté son soutien à Gianni Infantino, le président de la Fifa, lequel traverse une zone de turbulences, à quelques mois de la prochaine élection à la tête de l’instance, en mars 2027. Mais toutes les fédérations africaines ne sont pas forcément sur cette ligne.

stories.title: Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Zolani Tete was in training for a comeback fight when he was killed By Khanyisile Ngcobo ,Â Reporting from Johannesburg Â and Â Jude Winter ,Â BBC Sport Published 24 August 2026 Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday. Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital. One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges. Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014.

stories.title: Togo : les dessous du remaniement à la tête de l’armée et des renseignements
stories.summary: Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé a remanié en profondeur son appareil sécuritaire, le 17 août. Une refonte dictée autant par la menace jihadiste dans le nord du pays que par la volonté du président du Conseil de consolider sa mainmise sur l’armée.

stories.title: On Different Grounds review – Cupid’s-conspiracy romcom brings Nollywood and Bollywood together
stories.summary: Chemistry test … Abena Akuaba and Vineet Raina in On Different Grounds. Photograph: EvritFilms View image in fullscreen Chemistry test … Abena Akuaba and Vineet Raina in On Different Grounds. Photograph: EvritFilms Review On Different Grounds review – Cupid’s-conspiracy romcom brings Nollywood and Bollywood together Mildred Okwo’s earnest film about the conflicting romantic wishes in a Nigerian family struggles to connect with its promising premise I t’s a stretch for this Nigerian romcom to bill itself “the first Nollywood-Bollywood collaboration” based on the fact that it features, in Nimesh Diliprai Desai and Vineet Raina, two fringe Indian players on a sprawling wedding-invite list. But the two industries do indeed have much common ground, such as big-hearted family values and a penchant for grand gestural emotions that, in the case of Mildred Okwo’s somewhat heavy-footed film, trample on some promising concepts and narrative plausibility. Silk-tressed bachelorette Aurora (Abena Akuaba) is being browbeaten by her businessman dad Eyimofe (Bob-Manuel Udokwu) to marry snoozefest suitor Tobore (Ifeanyi Kalu).

stories.title: SOS Méditerranée alerte sur la hausse des violences en mer contre les migrants et les navires de sauvetage
stories.summary: L’ONG a recensé entre juin et juillet, à sept reprises au moins, des navires « liés à des acteurs libyens » et des « groupes armés », qui se sont approchés « à grande vitesse » de bateaux, ou les ont suivis des heures durant.

stories.title: Le canal de Suez, naissance et mort d’un mythe colonial, promesse d’un Orient où se mêlent aventure et fortune
stories.summary: « Suez, canal historique » (1/6). En 1869, la création d’un axe maritime permettant de relier la Méditerranée et la mer Rouge, exploité par les Français et les Britanniques, fascine l’Europe. D’abord symbole d’oppression coloniale pour le peuple égyptien, la voie d’eau devient un instrument d’émancipation quand le président Nasser annonce sa nationalisation, il y a tout juste soixante-dix ans, le 26 juillet 1956.

stories.title: Minerais critiques : comment l’Afrique cherche à rééquilibrer le rapport de force avec les pays importateurs
stories.summary: Une quinzaine de pays africains, producteurs de cobalt, de manganèse ou de lithium, ont décrété des embargos ou des quotas depuis 2023, pour contraindre les opérateurs extérieurs à investir localement dans la transformation de ces minéraux.

stories.title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says
stories.summary: Residents and rescuers search for bodies in the dump site in Conakry on 23 August. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Residents and rescuers search for bodies in the dump site in Conakry on 23 August. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state A ⁠landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to ⁠collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks. The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa . The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.

stories.title: Mali : entre Bamako et le FLA, les négociations secrètes qui ont permis un nouvel échange de prisonniers
stories.summary: Mali : entre Bamako et le FLA, les négociations secrètes qui ont permis un nouvel échange de prisonniers Vingt-deux soldats maliens ont été libérés le 23 août dans le cadre d’un échange avec le Front de libération de l’Azawad. Selon nos informations, un médiateur inhabituel a rendu possible ce nouvel accord. Les huit combattants du FLA libérés et réceptionnés près d’Anéfis par Ahmoudou Ag Asriw, un responsable du mouvement rebelle, le 23 août 2026. © DR Par Jeune Afrique Publié aujourd'hui à 09h00 Lecture : 3 minutes. Dimanche 23 août, vingt-deux militaires maliens ont été libérés dans le cadre d’un échange avec le Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA), qui a noué depuis avril une alliance officielle avec le Groupe de soutien à l’islam et aux musulmans (Jnim), affilié à Al-Qaida.

stories.title: En RD Congo, une première mission de vérification du cessez-le-feu dans l'Est
stories.summary: Publicité En RD Congo, une première mission de vérification du cessez-le-feu dans l'Est Afrique Alors que l'armée congolaise et le groupe politico-militaire AFC/M23, soutenu par le Rwanda, se sont mutuellement accusés d'exactions lundi, une première mission régionale de vérification d'un fragile cessez-le-feu entre les belligérants s'est déployée dans l'est de la République démocratique du Congo. Publié le : 24/08/2026 - 18:05 Modifié le : 24/08/2026 - 18:06 4 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 Des rebelles de l'AFC/M23 escortent des soldats et des policiers gouvernementaux à Goma, en République démocratique du Congo, le 30 janvier 2025. © Moses Sawasawa, AP L'armée congolaise et le groupe politico-militaire AFC/M23 se sont mutuellement accusés d'exactions, lundi 24 août. Dans le même temps, une première mission régionale de vérification d'un fragile cessez-le-feu entre les belligérants s'est déployée dans l'est de la République démocratique du Congo . L'est de la RD Congo est en proie à des conflits depuis plus de 30 ans. Le groupe armé antigouvernemental AFC/M23 s'y est emparé de vastes pans de territoires dans les provinces du Nord-Kivu et du Sud-Kivu depuis 2021, avec le soutien du Rwanda et son armée.

stories.title: Mali : le cercle restreint d’Alghabass Ag Intalla, l’architecte de l’alliance entre rebelles et jihadistes
stories.summary: Mali : le cercle restreint d’Alghabass Ag Intalla, l’architecte de l’alliance entre rebelles et jihadistes La libération de soldats maliens par le FLA marque un changement de stratégie du groupe rebelle. stories.summary: L’idée qui a attiré 100 millions de dollars : l’inspirant pari de cette étudiante ghanéenne À 22 ans, Nana Barwuah a fondé Afrovest, une plateforme qui met en relation des entreprises africaines et des investisseurs internationaux. stories.title: En Sierra Leone, les habitants des bidonvilles piégés par la montée de l’océan : « On est encerclés par la mer et par des torrents de pluie et d’eaux usées »
stories.summary: A Freetown, les précipitations et les marées transforment les quartiers proches de l’océan en vastes zones inondables. Faute d’équipements, des dizaines de milliers d’habitants vivent dangereusement au rythme des crues.

stories.title: Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
stories.summary: Image caption, Manasse Lomachar would like the discovery of gold to improve life in his village By Akisa Wandera Published 23 August 2026 A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks. When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; Â£205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor. And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps. It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.

stories.title: Le Togo confirme des poursuites contre deux réalisateurs français détenus
stories.summary: Publicité Le Togo confirme des poursuites contre deux réalisateurs français détenus Afrique Le gouvernement togolais a affirmé samedi que la justice disposait "d'indices graves et concordants" à l'encontre de Gaël Mocaër, Sebastian Perez Pezzani et Fred Vedomey, arrêtés le 27 juillet. stories.summary: Les Springboks affrontent à domicile les All Blacks néo-zélandais, samedi 22 août. Le premier d’une série de trois matchs très attendus. En dix ans, l’équipe nationale est parvenue à fédérer un large public, exauçant le rêve porté par Nelson Mandela en 1995.

stories.title: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’
stories.summary: A health worker preparing to disinfect the area during the burial of suspected Ebola victims in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face By Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia and Rachel Savage E very day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo , afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends. “More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.” View image in fullscreen A health worker’s protective gear is disinfected after handling the body of a suspected Ebola victim in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.” Ebola outbreak: five big questions Read more That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid. “I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses. Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.” View image in fullscreen A health worker dries disinfected boots in Bunia. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP U npaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.

stories.title: Africa: Inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit Convenes 27-28 August in Washington DC
stories.summary: Inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit Convenes 27-28 August in Washington DC ABIS Inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit set to 27-28 August at MGM National Harbor, Washington DC 21 August 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Business Investment Summit (Washington DC) Africa's business leaders will convene in Washington D.C., for the inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit (ABIS) 2026, taking place at MGM National Harbor 27–28 August 2026 as the centerpiece of Millennium Excellence Awards America . stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JCww The Lake Nyos incident was one of the deadliest natural disasters in Cameroon's history Image: AFP Advertisement "The Lake Nyos disaster took everybody by surprise. We had no warning signals before it ever took place," said Isaac Konfor Njilah, a Cameroonian geologist and head of a laboratory in the department of Earth Sciences at the University of Yaounde. On the night of August 21, 1986, Lake Nyos suddenly released a massive cloud of carbon dioxide that spread through nearby valleys and villages. The gas replaced oxygen, suffocating people and animals as they slept. Located in Cameroon's Northwest Region, about 315 kilometers (196 miles) northwest of Yaounde, Lake Nyos sits inside an ancient volcanic crater in the Oku volcanic field.

After July 30, when an estimated 72,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, there were further calls on social media for people to come to Fnideq for another mass crossing attempt in mid-August. That is despite the fact that around 100 people died in the July attempt and that most of those who crossed into Ceuta have since returned to Morocco. stories.title: Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The PDP's presidential candidate Olusegun Obasanjo swept to power in 1999, ushering in the return to democracy By Mansur Abubakar Reporting from Abuja Published 21 August 2026 Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction. A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive. A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box. It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades. For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.

Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images The Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid matters Editorial The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries F or months health experts have warned that the scale of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could surpass the one that swept west Africa in 2014-16. This week, the authorities in the DRC announced that a grim milestone has already been passed: at least 2,325 people have died from the virus, making it the deadliest of the country’s 17 outbreaks and the fastest-growing in history. There is no effective vaccine against Bundibugyo – a rare strain of the virus that spread fatally undetected during the spring, often being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

stories.title: Amanal Petros: From refugee to European champion
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5J4ps Amanal Petros, seen here celebrating his gold at the European Athletics Championships, first competed for Germany at the 2021 Olympic Games Image: Stefanos Kyriazis/NurPhoto/IMAGO Advertisement Amanal Petros stood in Birmingham's Victoria Square, the German flag draped over his shoulders and the gold medal resting on his chest. Eleven months after narrowly missing out on a World Championship title in Tokyo, the 31-year-old had just won his first major marathon . After roughly 25 of the 42 kilometers, Petros picked up the pace on an incline, breaking up the lead pack. He was able to savor the victory during the final 2 kilometers. He crossed the finish line in 2:09:11 — a record time for the men's marathon at the European Athletics Championships. "My goal was to wrap things up early," Petros said afterwards. "That worked out perfectly." The fact that Italian runner Pietro Riva finished just seven seconds behind him hardly reflected the commanding nature of the victory. "I had everything under control," Petros added.
